sessions.title: 1994 Annual Meeting Highlight Reel
sessions.summary: Highlights from the 1994 Berkshire Hathaway Annual meeting

sessions.title: Afternoon Session - 1994 Meeting
sessions.summary: Warren Buffett and Charlie Munger answer questions about Berkshire's investments in Salomon Brothers and Coca-Cola. (This session is audio only because a video recording is not available.)

sessions.title: Morning Session - 1994 Meeting
sessions.summary: Warren Buffett explains why it may not be evident that a reinsurance company is "swimming naked" until the "tide goes out."  Buffett also argues for a "steeply  progressive" consumption tax and calls derivatives a dangerous combination of "ignorance and borrowed money."

clips.title: Buffett and Munger's book recommendations
clips.summary: Warren Buffett and Charlie Munger discuss the best books they've read in the past year.

clips.title: Buffett's Blue Chip Stamps "wizardry"
clips.summary: Warren Buffett and Charlie Munger discuss how, with the trading stamp company Blue Chip Stamps, they presided over a "decline of 99 1/2 percent."

clips.title: "Charlie and I never have an opinion about the market"
clips.summary: Warren Buffett and Charlie Munger talk about why they don't calculate how the market is doing on any given day into their stock-buying decisions.

clips.title: Derivatives can be dangerous
clips.summary: Warren Buffett says derivatives could be a "recipe for trouble" because of the combination of "ignorance and borrowed money."

clips.title: How Berkshire holds onto its managers
clips.summary: Warren Buffett explains why, in order to retain managers, it's important to "find the .400 hitters and then not tell them how to swing."

clips.title: "We don't think we can improve on this group"
clips.summary: Warren Buffett and Charlie Munger explain why they don't foresee a time in the future when they would split Berkshire's stock.

clips.title: "We look at what the market says is the utility"
clips.summary: Warren Buffett weighs in on how he judges a product's usefulness.

clips.title: "We'd rather multiply by three than by pi"
clips.summary: Warren Buffett and Charlie Munger prefer to go with business that are easy for them to understand, because "you don't have to do exceptional things to get exceptional results."

clips.title: Why Buffett prefers to buy entire businesses
clips.summary: Warren Buffett says that if it were up to him, "we would own three times the number of businesses we own outright."

clips.title: "You judge management by two yardsticks"
clips.summary: Warren Buffett explains the main two factors he looks at when evaluating a company's management.

sessions.title: 1995 Annual Meeting Highlight Reel
sessions.summary: Highlights from the 1995 Berkshire Hathaway Annual meeting

sessions.title: Afternoon Session - 1995 Meeting
sessions.summary: Warren Buffett and Charlie Munger cover the "real" advantage of being rich, whether they're looking for international acquisitions, the secret to avoiding lawsuits, and what business schools really should be teaching.

sessions.title: Morning Session - 1995 Meeting
sessions.summary: Warren Buffett and Charlie Munger discuss Berkshire's acquisition of Helzberg's Diamonds, why "you don't have to make it back the way you lost it," and how even an "idiot" could successfully run Berkshire.

clips.title: Buffett and Munger on "the first threshold question"
clips.summary: Warren Buffett and Charlie Munger reveal the first test a potential Berkshire investment must pass.

clips.title: Buffett prefers "obvious" business decisions
clips.summary: Warren Buffett and Charlie Munger say they like to make investment decisions where the decision is so easy that there's no need to do complicated calculations.

clips.title: Finding the right "lord of the castle"
clips.summary: Warren Buffett and Charlie Munger talk about the characteristics they look for in managers.

clips.title: How Buffett acquired Helzberg's Diamonds
clips.summary: Warren Buffett tells the story of how a random run-in with Barnett Helzberg on the street led to Berkshire Hathaway buying Helzberg's Diamonds.

clips.title: "I think Salomon's going to be around for a long time"
clips.summary: Four years out from the Treasury bond scandal at the investment firm Salomon Brothers, Warren Buffett says he's hopeful for the company's future.

clips.title: Is growing media attention a distraction for Buffett?
clips.summary: Warren Buffett responds to a shareholder's concern that his increasing fame may cause his focus to waver.

clips.title: "It's not that complicated to figure out where it makes sense to put money"
clips.summary: Warren Buffett and Charlie Munger say business and investing are a whole lot simpler than business schools and consultants try to make them.

clips.title: "Less than likely" Berkshire will buy outside the U.S.
clips.summary: Warren Buffett explains why it would be challenging for Berkshire to buy businesses based outside of the United States.

clips.title: "Look twice at companies" with confusing accounting
clips.summary: Warren Buffett and Charlie Munger say if you can't understand a company's accounting, stay away.

clips.title: "Most moats aren't worth a damn"
clips.summary: Warren Buffett explains the analogy of the "castle and moat" that he uses to evaluate businesses.

clips.title: Munger: An "idiot" could successfully run Berkshire
clips.summary: Warren Buffett says Berkshire Hathaway has a big advantage over other companies in that it's not only willing to buy partial stakes in companies, but it's also willing to buy whole companies. He and Charlie Munger say Berkshire will continue to run smoothly "long after" they're gone.

clips.title: Newspapers "still making exceptional money"
clips.summary: Despite some economic declines in the newspaper industry, Warren Buffett says he would still rather buy "a newspaper in a single newspaper town" than most other businesses. Charlie Munger, though, tempers his enthusiasm.

clips.title: Rich people can get "antagonistic" toward others
clips.summary: Warren Buffett talks about how wealthy people need to check themselves against emotions like hatred and envy.

clips.title: Should Berkshire start another Borsheims store?
clips.summary: Warren Buffett talks about how Borsheims is different from jewelers like Helzberg's and why it has advantages as a one-location company.

clips.title: The secret to avoiding lawsuits
clips.summary: For an enormous company, Berkshire Hathaway doesn't get sued all that often. Warren Buffett and Charlie Munger reveal how they keep the company out of court.

clips.title: Why Buffett and Munger don't trust financial projections
clips.summary: Warren Buffett and Charlie Munger explain why, despite being offered numerous projections, they don't use them when making investment decisions.

clips.title: Why are Buffett's family members on the board?
clips.summary: Warren Buffett explains why having Buffetts on Berkshire's board of trustees helps ensure the company's future stability.

clips.title: Why shareholders aren't given video of Berkshire meetings
clips.summary: Warren Buffett says if Berkshire gave out videotapes of the annual meeting, some shareholders might not show up in person ... with their wallets.

clips.title: "You ought to be doing what you like"
clips.summary: Warren and Buffett get philosophical about living in the present.

sessions.title: 1996 Annual Meeting Highlight Reel
sessions.summary: Highlights from the 1996 Berkshire Hathaway Annual meeting

sessions.title: Afternoon Session - 1996 Meeting
sessions.summary: Warren Buffett and Charlie Munger discuss why they think portfolio diversification is a "protection against ignorance," explain why they're fearful of change, and argue that people rewarded by capitalism have an obligation to help people who don't do as well.

sessions.title: Morning Session - 1996 Meeting
sessions.summary: Warren Buffett and Charlie Munger discuss in detail why Berkshire created its lower-priced B shares and answer a number of questions about the new stock class. They also explain why the company isn't a "one-man show."

clips.title: "Berkshire is not a one-man show"
clips.summary: Warren Buffett and Charlie Munger explain why they're confident Berkshire will be successful long after they are gone.

clips.title: Buffett and Munger address capitalism's shortcomings
clips.summary: Warren Buffett and Charlie Munger weigh in on the inequality created by the market system.

clips.title: Buffett and Munger on diversification
clips.summary: Warren Buffett and Charlie Munger explain why they believe diversifying your investment portfolio makes very little sense for anyone that knows what they are doing

clips.title: Buffett and Munger's views on downsizing
clips.summary: Warren Buffett and Charlie Munger share their opinions on the trends towards downsizing and offshoring.

clips.title: Buffett on Ben Graham's investing principles
clips.summary: Warren Buffett recommends Benjamin Graham's book, "The Intelligent Investor," and outlines what he considers Graham's three most important ideas.

clips.title: Buffett on insurance "float"
clips.summary: Warren Buffett explains the idea behind insurance float and how it has worked in Berkshire's favor.

clips.title: Buffett on the future of World Book
clips.summary: Warren Buffett gives his take on how World Book Encyclopedia will fare in the electronic age and weighs in on whether he'd ever sell the business.

clips.title: Buffett on the price of the Class B
clips.summary: Warren Buffett explains how Berkshire came to a decision on the cost of the Class B shares.

clips.title: How Class B shares compare to A
clips.summary: Warren Buffett explains the ways in which Berkshire's Class A shares have an advantage over the new Class B.

clips.title: How does the issuance of Class B shares affect A shareholders?
clips.summary: Warren Buffett addresses the concern that the new Class B shares may hurt Class A shareholders.

clips.title: "It's still a very fine business"
clips.summary: Warren Buffett shares his views on the future of the newspaper industry.

clips.title: No layoffs because of "a drop in volume"
clips.summary: Warren Buffett shares his views on how new capital going into reinsurance carriers will impact Berkshire's companies.

clips.title: "We really feel the fairer, the better"
clips.summary: Warren Buffett explains why he has a different view than most managers on his company's stock prices.

clips.title: What Buffett looks for in annual reports
clips.summary: Warren Buffett describes how reading companies' annual reports helps him make investment decisions.

clips.title: When to invest in a great company
clips.summary: Warren Buffett describes the criteria he uses to evaluate companies and why price isn't always the most important factor.

clips.title: Why Buffett is change-averse
clips.summary: Warren Buffett explains why investing in businesses that are likely to change a lot "scares the hell" out of him and Charlie Munger.

clips.title: Why create Class B shares?
clips.summary: Leading up to the board of directors' vote on adding Class B shares, Warren Buffett explains the thinking behind the Class B.

clips.title: Will Bill Gates join Berkshire's board?
clips.summary: Warren Buffett explains why he doesn't foresee Bill Gates becoming part of Berkshire.

clips.title: "You get a lot of mediocrity"
clips.summary: Warren Buffett shares his views on good management and why the CEOs of the Fortune 500 aren't like an Olympic team.

sessions.title: 1997 Annual Meeting Highlight Reel
sessions.summary: Highlights from the 1997 Berkshire Hathaway Annual meeting

sessions.title: Afternoon Session - 1997 Meeting
sessions.summary: Warren Buffett and Charlie Munger offer a detailed explanation of what they look for when deciding whether to buy a business and how they try to avoid "jerks." They also cover the need for a large "margin of safety" and admit they made a mistake on pharmaceutical stocks.

sessions.title: Morning Session - 1997 Meeting
sessions.summary: Warren Buffett and Charlie Munger explain why investors shouldn't be afraid of volatility, how they know in five minutes if they want to buy a company, and complain that many money managers are getting "a lot for nothing."

clips.title: America's economy "encourages" adaptation
clips.summary: Warren Buffett explains why he's still optimistic about the future of American industry.

clips.title: Buffett and Munger on the capital gains tax
clips.summary: Warren Buffett and Charlie Munger give their  views on a "fair" capital gains tax rate and the responsibility a society has to provide for its less privileged citizens.

clips.title: Buffett's "five minute test"
clips.summary: Warren Buffett describes his process for quickly judging whether or not he's interested in investing in a particular company.

clips.title: Buffett's "normal day"
clips.summary: Warren Buffett explains why his day-to-day work life, which he loves, is "the most boring job to anyone watching it."

clips.title: How Buffett became a better investor than his mentor
clips.summary: Warren Buffett and Charlie Munger explain how Benjamin Graham and Phil Fisher influenced their investing philosophy and why Buffett was ultimately able to out-perform Graham.

clips.title: How history shapes Munger's beliefs
clips.summary: Charlie Munger often cites Aristotle and other historical figures when talking about his life and business philosophies. He gives his take on the importance of studying history.

clips.title: How investing is similar to choosing a spouse
clips.summary: Charlie Munger and Warren Buffett discuss opportunity cost and how it comes into play in making investment decisions.

clips.title: Is McDonald's an "inevitable" company?
clips.summary: Warren Buffett responds to an investor's question about whether McDonald's is a business that is certain to dominate its industry.

clips.title: "It's share of mind that counts"
clips.summary: Warren Buffett talks about the importance of how consumers think about a company.

clips.title: "Learn from the other guys' mistakes"
clips.summary: Warren Buffett and Charlie Munger share their strategies for avoiding mistakes and explain why most of their errors have been "mistakes of omission."

clips.title: "Mistake" not to buy drug companies
clips.summary: Warren Buffett and Charlie Munger give their take on the pharmaceutical industry and why Berkshire hasn't invested in it.

clips.title: Money managers have gotten "something for nothing"
clips.summary: Warren Buffett explains why he's just as critical of money managers as he was five years ago.

clips.title: Most conversations end "in the middle of somebody's first sentence"
clips.summary: Warren Buffett explains how he makes investment decisions and why he quickly weeds out most companies presented to him.

clips.title: Slowdown for stocks coming?
clips.summary: Warren Buffett and Charlie Munger assess the chances that stock growth will slow over the coming decade.

clips.title: "The stock market is there to serve you and not to instruct you"
clips.summary: Warren Buffett explains the way he thinks about stock market risk and why investors should love "wild swings."

clips.title: "There are a lot more interesting things that are going to happen"
clips.summary: Warren Buffett talks about why he hasn't written a book yet.

clips.title: Why Buffett doesn't invest in Intel and Microsoft
clips.summary: Warren Buffett explains why he doesn't invest in technology companies even though they're growing rapidly.

sessions.title: 1998 Annual Meeting Highlight Reel
sessions.summary: Highlights from the 1998 Berkshire Hathaway Annual meeting

sessions.title: Afternoon Session - 1998 Meeting
sessions.summary: Warren Buffett and Charlie Munger take aim at big compensation for mediocre CEOs, explain why Berkshire's decentralization is "just short of total abdication," dismiss "due diligence" as a waste of money that misses the point, and promise they will "wait indefinitely."

sessions.title: Morning Session - 1998 Meeting
sessions.summary: Warren Buffett and Charlie Munger reveal the "secret of life,"  remind investors there's no "degree of difficulty" bonus, and assure shareholders Berkshire would be fine even if it simultaneously lost all its top managers.

clips.title: Believe markets are efficient? Go right ahead
clips.summary: Warren Buffett points out that Berkshire has an advantage: everyone else believes market prices instantly reflect all available information.

clips.title: Berkshire has people "leagues ahead of Charlie and me"
clips.summary: Warren Buffett explains why he's confident his successors will run Berkshire capably after he and Charlie Munger are gone.

clips.title: Buffett and Munger on inheritance
clips.summary: Warren Buffett and Charlie Munger discuss the issues around leaving money to children, including whether money ruins heirs and if there should be an inheritance tax.

clips.title: Buffett on what is important and what is knowable
clips.summary: Warren Buffett and Charlie Munger explain why they focus on what certain companies will look like over the long term instead of trying to make predictions about where the economy is headed.

clips.title: "Buy a stock that you don't ever want to sell"
clips.summary: Berkshire doesn't sell any of its stock holdings very often, but it can happen. Warren Buffett lists some situations that can make him a seller.

clips.title: "Get it corrected and get back to sleep"
clips.summary: Warren Buffett explains why he and Charlie Munger don't worry about much. He says even in tough times, they have a lot of fun with their business.

clips.title: How Buffett assesses a company's value
clips.summary: Warren Buffett answers a shareholder's question on how he estimates how much a given company is worth.

clips.title: Operating from a "Norman Rockwell frame of mind"
clips.summary: Warren Buffett talks about how he and Charlie Munger like to buy businesses with a "homey" character to them.

clips.title: Phil Fisher's "scuttlebutt" method
clips.summary: The "scuttlebutt" method refers to the process of getting information about companies and products from as many sources as possible. Warren Buffett discusses "scuttlebutt" and the ways he now goes about investigating businesses.

clips.title: Public education "needs fixing"
clips.summary: Warren Buffett and Charlie Munger discuss the challenges of the public school system and give differing views on vouchers.

clips.title: "That is a seven or eight foot bar that I can't clear"
clips.summary: Warren Buffett explains why, despite admiring tech companies and their founders, he doesn't invest in the tech industry.

clips.title: "The B has worked out as well as possible"
clips.summary: In 1996, Berkshire Hathaway started issuing Class B shares with a lower price in dollars than the never-split Class A shares. Warren Buffett says he's "happy with the present situation."

clips.title: "The secret of life is weak competition"
clips.summary: Warren Buffett explains why it doesn't help you much if you're a genius competing only with other geniuses.

clips.title: There's no "degree of difficulty" factor in investing
clips.summary: Warren Buffett explains why he prefers to stay away from more difficult investments.

clips.title: "We don't have any strategic plan"
clips.summary: Warren Buffett says Berkshire doesn't have any sort of "predetermined course of action" for which of its businesses will become the largest.

clips.title: What Buffett looks for in an annual report
clips.summary: Warren Buffett values candor when reading annual reports, saying it turns him off when companies use "a standardized bunch of popular jargon."

clips.title: "What bothers me is when companies pay a lot of money for mediocrity"
clips.summary: Warren Buffett gives his views on executive compensation, explaining why he doesn't mind paying big money for good performance.

clips.title: What's the difference between the A and B shares?
clips.summary: Warren Buffett explains the economic and voting rights differences between Berkshire's Class A and Class B shares, saying they are "very equivalent investment choices."

clips.title: Why there's no "due diligence" in Berkshire deals
clips.summary: Warren Buffett says having lawyers look over all the details of a company he's going to purchase is a waste of time and money.

clips.title: Will the internet help Berkshire's businesses?
clips.summary: Warren Buffett and Charlie Munger talk about the opportunities—and threats—posed to their companies by the internet.

clips.title: Y2K problem won't have a huge impact on Berkshire
clips.summary: Widespread concern about the Y2K computer bug issue spread in the years leading up to the year 2000. Warren Buffett says he's not too worried.

sessions.title: 1999 Annual Meeting Highlight Reel
sessions.summary: Highlights from the 1999 Berkshire Hathaway Annual meeting

sessions.title: Afternoon Session - 1999 Meeting
sessions.summary: Warren Buffett and Charlie Munger continue to explain why they're not buying hot internet stocks, dismiss efficient market theory as "silly," and offer advice on starting out as an investor.

sessions.title: Morning Session - 1999 Meeting
sessions.summary: At the height of the internet bubble, Warren Buffett and Charlie Munger defend their decision not to buy tech stocks. They also reveal what may have contributed to the failure of Berkshire's big bid for LTCM, and criticize "corrupt" stock option accounting and smart people taking dumb risks with derivatives.

clips.title: Benefits of buying General Re won't be felt "in the short term"
clips.summary: Berkshire bought the reinsurance company General Re in 1998. Warren Buffett says he doesn't expect to feel the benefits of the acquisition for a few more years.

clips.title: Best books Buffett and Munger read this year
clips.summary: Warren Buffett and Charlie Munger recommend several of their favorite nonfiction reads from the past year.

clips.title: Buffett on evaluating businesses' "moats"
clips.summary: Warren Buffett explains why it's important to look at the companies' "moats," their ability to maintain an advantage over their competitors.

clips.title: Buffett on stock options as compensation
clips.summary: Warren Buffett discusses why it's necessary to account for the "real cost" of using stock options.

clips.title: Buffett on the risks LTCM's management took
clips.summary: Warren Buffett says it's "fascinating" to him that smart and experienced people could lose so much money by making risky investments in derivatives.

clips.title: Buffett wants shareholders who are "in sync" with Berkshire
clips.summary: Warren Buffett says he wants people who own Berkshire stock to have the same philosophical framework he does when it comes to investing.

clips.title: Buffett's advice on making big money
clips.summary: Warren Buffett explains the process he would go through if he were getting out of school today with $10,000 to invest.

clips.title: Buffett's long-distance rescue bid for Long-Term Capital Management
clips.summary: Warren Buffett discusses the near-collapse of the hedge fund Long-Term Capital Management, which was ultimately bailed out by the Federal Reserve. Warren Buffett describes Berkshire's unsuccessful bid to rescue the firm, which occurred when Buffett and Bill Gates were on a trip together.

clips.title: Efficient market theory is "silly"
clips.summary: Warren Buffett criticizes the efficient market theory, the idea that existing share prices fully reflect all available information.

clips.title: How Berkshire adds value to its subsidiaries
clips.summary: Warren Buffett says Berkshire enables its subsidiary companies to "spend a hundred percent of their time focused on what counts."

clips.title: How can Berkshire capitalize on the internet?
clips.summary: Warren Buffett says the trust people have in the Berkshire Hathaway name will help Berkshire do business on the internet.

clips.title: How will the internet impact business?
clips.summary: At the height of the "dot-com" bubble, Warren Buffett looks ahead to how the internet could change the retail industry.

clips.title: "I don't have to bet" on technology companies
clips.summary: Warren Buffett says he would rather invest in companies like Coca-Cola instead of companies like Microsoft because he's "perfectly willing to trade away a big payoff for a certain payoff."

clips.title: "It was a mistake" to sell McDonald's
clips.summary: Warren Buffett explains why he decided to sell McDonald's and discusses the importance of conducting "postmortems" after making business decisions.

clips.title: Keep asking, "Why? Why? Why? Why?"
clips.summary: Warren Buffett and Charlie Munger talk about the importance of extensively reading and talking to people when learning about businesses and investing.

clips.title: Successors "would be ready to run Berkshire tomorrow morning"
clips.summary: Warren Buffett explains why he doesn't need to groom his potential successors.

clips.title: "The money makes no difference after a moderate level"
clips.summary: Warren Buffett says the most important thing in life and work is "who you do it with."

clips.title: "We look at change as a threat"
clips.summary: Warren Buffett and Charlie Munger talk about why they seek out businesses they think will look the same in 10 or 20 years.

clips.title: Why hasn't Buffett invested in communications?
clips.summary: Warren Buffett says he stays away from the communications industry because he has "no insights that I bring that I think are in any way superior."

sessions.title: 2000 Annual Meeting Highlight Reel
sessions.summary: Highlights from the 2000 Berkshire Hathaway Annual meeting

sessions.title: Afternoon Session - 2000 Meeting
sessions.summary: Warren Buffett defends a big retirement package for Coca-Cola's outgoing CEO. He also identifies an unexpected factor in spiraling CEO pay, explains why buying Berkshire Hathaway was a "terrible mistake," and admits he's a little "crazy" because he doesn't mind paying taxes.

sessions.title: Morning Session - 2000 Meeting
sessions.summary: Warren Buffett and Charlie Munger are criticized by some shareholders for underperforming tech stocks the previous year, discuss the relationship between "look-through" book value and intrinsic value, and detail what would prompt Berkshire to pay a dividend.

clips.title: Berkshire is the "Metropolitan Museum of Businesses"
clips.summary: Warren Buffett explains that Berkshire Hathaway's businesses are like "paintings" because company managers are given the freedom to create their own masterpieces.

clips.title: Birds, hands, and bushes: The first investment primer
clips.summary: Warren Buffett goes back 2600 years to find an important investing lesson in the moral of a very well-known fable.

clips.title: Buffett: This is the best book on how I invest
clips.summary: Warren Buffett says people who write books about his views on investing are sometimes looking for "mechanistic things or formulas" that don't exist. He names the book he thinks best encapsulates his philosophy.

clips.title: Buffett and Gates "hit it off immediately"
clips.summary: Warren Buffett explains how he and Bill Gates initially became friends.

clips.title: Buffett on what "understanding" a business means
clips.summary: Warren Buffett explains that when he says he doesn't understand tech stocks, he means he doesn't understand where the tech industry will be in ten years.

clips.title: Business schools themselves are good businesses
clips.summary: Warren Buffett explains why Harvard Business School and Stanford Business School have positioned themselves in such a way that the more they cost, the more people think the education is worth.

clips.title: Growth and value are not distinct categories
clips.summary: Wall Street analysts often frame "value investing" and "growth investing" as two different strategies. Warren Buffett says this is the wrong way to look at it because both value and growth factor into any investment.

clips.title: How will the internet impact newspapers?
clips.summary: Warren Buffett speculates about the future of the newspaper industry, saying no one really knows "how it's going to play out."

clips.title: "I'm no good on macro questions"
clips.summary: Warren Buffett explains why he doesn't take trends in the global economy into consideration when making investment decisions.

clips.title: "It does pay to have the right models"
clips.summary: Warren Buffett and Charlie Munger discuss the importance of having good role models and how the "eminent dead" are some of the best ones.

clips.title: Munger: "If you mix raisins with turds, they're still turds"
clips.summary: Warren Buffett and Charlie Munger talk about the dangers of the widespread speculation in the internet and tech industries.

clips.title: The internet is "probably a net negative" for capitalists
clips.summary: Warren Buffett and Charlie Munger talk about how the internet will impact Berkshire, the average company, and society as a whole.

clips.title: "The original purchase of Berkshire was a terrible mistake"
clips.summary: Warren Buffett explains that he bought Berkshire Hathaway because of an "irritating" move by its then-president, Seabury Stanton - and says it's "interesting that a wrong decision has been made to work out so well."

clips.title: "We are enormously risk averse"
clips.summary: Warren Buffett is always thinking about what could go wrong, as he sees businesses as economic castles that are "subject to marauders."

clips.title: "We have this quirk" when it comes to selling businesses
clips.summary: Warren Buffett explains why Berkshire doesn't sell its businesses "simply because we get offered a fancy price for something."

clips.title: "We've got the best job in the world"
clips.summary: Warren Buffett and Charlie Munger explain why neither one of them would have any interest in working in the public sector.

clips.title: Will Berkshire take advantage of the weak dollar?
clips.summary: Warren Buffett explains why Berkshire doesn't try to predict future currency moves when it considers buying stock.

clips.title: Will the internet hurt Berkshire's businesses?
clips.summary: Warren Buffett and Charlie Munger assess about how the internet threatens some of Berkshire's holdings, like newspapers and World Book.

sessions.title: 2001 Annual Meeting Highlight Reel
sessions.summary: Highlights from the 2001 Berkshire Hathaway Annual meeting

sessions.title: Afternoon Session - 2001 Meeting
sessions.summary: Warren Buffett and Charlie Munger discuss why selling short is "tempting" but "painful," reveal what's better than years of experience, warn against "potential dynamite" in derivatives, and share the most important piece of advice Buffett gives to young people.

sessions.title: Morning Session - 2001 Meeting
sessions.summary: In the wake of the bursting of the tech bubble, Warren Buffett and Charlie Munger discuss whether the internet remains a threat to retailers. They also reflect on the big, but unseen, costs of "blown opportunities," and Buffett reveals what his doctor has been telling him.

clips.title: Berkshire's long-term advantages
clips.summary: Warren Buffett explains why he believes Berkshire Hathaway will remain competitive for years to come.

clips.title: Buffett's expectations for Executive Jet
clips.summary: Warren Buffett outlines his hopes for Executive Jet's long-term growth.

clips.title: "Growth and value, they're indistinguishable"
clips.summary: Warren Buffett explains why he doesn't accept the commonly-held belief that growth and value stocks are "contrasting asset classes."

clips.title: How Executive Jet has done better than airlines
clips.summary: Warren Buffett discusses how Executive Jet successfully passed labor costs onto its customers and the importance for airlines to keep their costs in line with their competitors.

clips.title: How to teach kids about money
clips.summary: Warren Buffett and Charlie Munger talk about giving children a good financial education and the importance of also teaching them that "life is more than being shrewd at passive wealth accumulation."

clips.title: How would Buffett invest a small sum today?
clips.summary: Warren Buffett explains the process he would use if he were just starting out again in investing.

clips.title: Internet stocks were "a huge trap for the public"
clips.summary: In the wake of the internet bubble's deflation, Warren Buffett sees a "diminished" threat to traditional "brick and mortar" retailers and "gullible" investors.

clips.title: Mistakes "show up in opportunity costs"
clips.summary: Charlie Munger and Warren Buffett admit their biggest errors are often "mistakes of omission" that don't show up in Berkshire's balance sheet.

clips.title: "This is a scummy way to keep the books"
clips.summary: Warren Buffett and Charlie Munger criticize excessively optimistic investment gain projections for pension funds.

clips.title: Buffett: America needs a 'wartime' strategy for clean energy
clips.summary: Warren Buffett argues that the U.S. needs to "reorient the resources" of the country to achieve energy transformation, just as it did to win World War II. But he worries it may not be possible to recreate that kind of effort under our current democratic system.

clips.title: Buffett: We don't own too many Apple shares
clips.summary: Warren Buffett dismisses criticism that Berkshire's portfolio is dominated by its Apple shares, arguing the position should be evaluated in the broader context of both the stocks and companies it owns. In addition, he says, it's a "better business" than any of its fully-owned subsidiaries. On top of that, Charlie Munger thinks experts are wrong to advocate for what he calls the "deworsification" of investments.

clips.title: Buffett rules out Occidental Petroleum acquisition
clips.summary: In the middle of a discussion about Occidental Petroleum's oil drilling in the Permian Basin, Warren Buffett definitively rules out a Berkshire bid to take control of the oil giant, squelching speculation prompted by its steadily growing OXY stake.

clips.title: Buffett worries about Paramount's future in streaming business
clips.summary: Warren Buffett won't say why Berkshire Hathaway owns a stake in Paramount Global despite his concerns about heavy price competition in the unpredictable video streaming market.

clips.title: 'Catastrophic' if FDIC didn't backstop SVB deposits
clips.summary: Warren Buffett explains why he thinks its was "inevitable" and necessary for the FDIC to guarantee all deposits at the failed Silicon Valley Bank, even if they were above the formal $250,000 limit.

clips.title: Elon Musk doesn't need to 'overestimate' himself
clips.summary: Charlie Munger thinks Elon Musk doesn't need to "overestimate" himself because he is a very talented dreamer who "likes taking on the impossible job and doing it." He and Warren Buffett agree they would rather tackle easy jobs.

clips.title: Hard to predict if there will be electric vehicle winners
clips.summary: Warren Buffett and Charlie Munger think the automobile industry's transition to electric vehicles is fascinating, but are reluctant to invest, with Buffett saying, "I think I know where Apple is going to be in five or ten years, but I don't know where the car companies are going to be in five or ten years."

clips.title: 'I do not sign a will until my children have read it'
clips.summary: Warren Buffett says parents are making a terrible mistake if their grown children are not involved in their estate planning.

clips.title: Munger: I accept that my grandchildren won't think the way I do
clips.summary: Charlie Munger says he tries to set a good example for his grandchildren but is "philosophical" about them not thinking exactly the way he does. He also knows he needs to "pretend that I like some of the boyfriends and girlfriends I don't like."

clips.title: Munger: 'Old-fashioned intelligence works pretty well'
clips.summary: Charlie Munger is skeptical of some of the artificial intelligence hype, while Warren Buffett is worried that it can't be "uninvented" if things go wrong.

clips.title: Never make an emotional investing decision
clips.summary: Warren Buffett and Charlie Munger explain why you should be a "no emotion" person when it comes to making financial decisions.

clips.title: 'Not everything that should happen does happen'
clips.summary: After UK regulators move to block Microsoft's proposed acquisition of video game maker Activision Blizzard, Warren Buffett won't say whether he has given up on his arbitrage bet that the deal would go through. But he acknowledges it is not looking good, despite Microsoft's "more than halfway" efforts to address antitrust concerns on both sides of the Atlantic.

clips.title: 'Poor messaging' is making Americans worry about their bank deposits
clips.summary: Warren Buffett argues Washington should abandon its stated, but not always observed, $250,000 limit on bank deposit insurance and explicitly guarantee that no American will lose any money due to the failure of a U.S. bank.

clips.title: Raiders won't have enough money to target Berkshire after Buffett
clips.summary: Warren Buffett says he does think about what will happen when he no longer controls Berkshire, but doesn't "worry enormously" because no one will have enough money to take over the company.

clips.title: U.S.-China economic tensions are 'stupid, stupid, stupid'
clips.summary: Warren Buffett and Charlie Munger call on the leaders of both the U.S. and China to step back from the growing economic tensions between the two countries and embrace mutually-beneficial trading.

clips.title: 'We love our business'
clips.summary: In response to a question about the "hardest part of his business," Warren Buffett says he "works with the greatest group of people he can imagine" in "ideal working conditions."

clips.summary: Warren Buffett tells CNBC's Becky Quick it is a difficult time to find suitable investments for Berkshire, in part because there are fewer businesses he "understands" as technology becomes more complicated. But, he says, it's still possible to find "one that you know makes sense," as Apple did.

clips.title: Buffett 'celebrates' Greg Abel and Apple's Tim Cook
clips.summary: Speaking from his seat on the floor of the arena, Warren Buffett praises the board's decision to name Greg Abel as his CEO successor and thanks outgoing Apple CEO Tim Cook for contributing to the great success of Berkshire's equity investment in the computer company.

clips.title: Buffett's 'number' is retired
clips.summary: As the meeting is beginning, a Warren Buffett "jersey" with a large 60, reflecting his 60 years as Berkshire Hathaway's CEO, is raised to the rafters of Omaha's CHI Health arena in a symbolic number retirement.

clips.title: Court win 'resets the stage' in fight over wildfires liability
clips.summary: Greg Abel recounts an important Oregon appellate court victory as Berkshire challenges what it sees as unjust liability claims for wildfires in 2020.

clips.title: 'Depends on the price'
clips.summary: Ajit Jain explains why deciding whether or not to insure ships crossing the Strait of Hormuz in the midst of the Iran war is essentially answering one question: what would be the reward for taking the risk.

clips.title: How Abel will handle underperforming managers
clips.summary: Berkshire Hathaway prides itself on its decentralized structure for subsidiaries, but Greg Abel discusses when and how it would be appropriate for him to "engage and have a discussion."

clips.title: How Berkshire finally won coveted deal with Japan's Tokio Marine
clips.summary: Ajit Jain describes how Berkshire eventually did its 2026 deal with Japan's highly respected insurer Tokio Marine after years of trying.

clips.title: Warren Buffett's Mid-Meeting Live Interview
clips.summary: As the meeting's lunch break is ending, Warren Buffett sits down with CNBC's Becky Quick for a live interview streamed on CNBC.com and shown on screens for shareholders in the arena. They discuss why Buffett doesn't think it is a great time for Berkshire to make major investments and his concerns about the future impacts of AI, among other topics.

clips.title: 'We've never had people in a more gambling mood than now'
clips.summary: Warren Buffett says the growing popularity of "gambling' in the financial markets is distorting prices and making it harder to find attractive investments.

clips.title: Who does Abel cheer for when the the USA and Canadian hockey teams face off?
clips.summary: CEO Greg Abel, a Canadian who is becoming an American citizen, describes the compromise he found when hockey teams from the two countries play each other.

clips.title: Why it's important to 'just say no'
clips.summary: Ajit Jain and Greg Abel explain why their "base case" response to any proposed deal is "no."

clips.title: Will anyone be Greg's 'Charlie?'
clips.summary: Greg Abel says Berkshire will "endure as a team but clearly with leadership."
